extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy (readers of Plato's Republic)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt/commentary on Plato's Republic outlining standards for a well-ordered State and the virtues of the soul (wisdom, courage, temperance, justice), plus prescriptions for education, guardianship, gender roles, and social organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: First duty then happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: First duty, then happiness, is the natural order of our moral ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage states that the utilitarian principle (greatest happiness) is useful as a corrective but is not the historical basis of morality. The State's chief aim in founding itself is not to make citizens happy (they are guardians, not holiday-makers); duty precedes individual happiness and forms the natural moral order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatest-happiness principle is secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The greatest happiness’ principle is not the true foundation of ethics; it is the second principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although utility may be co-extensive with right in many cases and useful for application, 'happiness' is ambiguous and too closely associated with comforts rather than the 'goods of the soul'. The commentator argues that the greatest happiness principle lacks the definiteness and sacredness of 'truth' and 'right'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right and truth as highest aims of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Right and truth are the highest aims of government as well as of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political measures should not lose sight of right and truth because of temporal expediency; they appeal to a nation's better mind. Even in commercial/utilitarian states, ideas and ideals remain powerful; statesmen must be above ambition and value national character over material comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: State should be limited in size (Greek model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The State should be limited in size, following the traditional model of a Greek city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary notes a requirement (drawn from Aristotle and the Politics) that small city-states are preferable and that the smallness of Hellas' cities is converted into a principle for the proper size of a State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour / 'every one having his own'
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice in the State consists in 'every one having his own' — the division of labour and each person doing his own business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates defines justice as each class and each part of the soul doing its proper work. The text warns against roles being mixed (e.g., a cobbler becoming a guardian), saying great evil arises when individuals perform another's business; injustice is insubordination of inferior elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisdom (politic) as a civic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Wisdom: the State will be wise because politic — the skill of advising about the interests of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wisdom is concentrated in the guardians (a small ruling class); it is distinct from technical crafts (carpentry etc.) and is the form of skill concerned with the common good. If the rulers possess wisdom, the whole State will be wise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage (political) defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage is 'the never-failing salvation of the opinions which law and education have prescribed concerning dangers' (political or civilized courage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the dyers' analogy (education as ground, laws as dye), courage is that fixed right opinion about dangers that persists despite pleasure, pain or fear. It is distinguished from mere animal courage or a higher intellectual courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance as harmony/mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance suggests harmony: the better principle in a man masters the worse; a 'master of himself' is harmony among parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance is a quality distributed through the whole State (harmony between classes) and in the individual (friendship of ruling and subject principles). It is akin to justice but often describes a part or harmony rather than the whole-order quality of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as universal order (right man in right place)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is the perfect order by which all natures and classes do their own business — the right man in the right place, and co-operation of all citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice is presented as the supreme or foundational virtue: universal, abstract, and the condition that binds wisdom, courage and temperance into a harmonious whole. It is contrasted with injustice, which is insubordination and likened to disease in the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four cardinal virtues enumerated
rubrics_metrics.description: The State (and the individual) will contain the four cardinal virtues: wisdom, courage, temperance, justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage collects the four virtues as the central evaluative dimensions of the Republic's polity and of individual moral quality; one (justice) is treated as supreme over the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three parts of the soul: rational, irascible, concupiscent
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul is divided into three parts: the rational (reason), the irascible or spirited (passion), and the concupiscent (desire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's psychology ties each part to a civic class (counsellor, warrior, producers). The commentary uses examples (thirst vs. reason, Leontius story) to show the distinct impulses and how 'spirit' allies with reason against desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for distinct faculties: cannot produce contradictory effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed criterion: the same faculty cannot produce contradictory effects in the same relation and at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To distinguish faculties, Plato argues by difference in working: if two impulses can produce opposite responses (e.g., thirst 'drink' vs. reason 'do not drink') they must spring from distinct principles. Exceptions and modifications (like 'angry thirst') must be excluded for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education fixes right opinion (dyers' analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is the ground upon which laws (the dye) fix right opinions; properly laid education makes convictions resistant to pleasure or pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the dyers' image, the text argues that early education and law together 'fix' opinions (colours) so that neither 'soap of pleasure' nor 'lye of pain' will wash them out. Thus education/law are central tools for forming civic courage and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender equality of function when natures equal
rubrics_metrics.description: If women share the same nature and aptitudes as men for certain tasks, they should receive the same education and perform the same employments (music, gymnastics, art of war).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates argues against assuming wholesale difference of sexes: differences may be partial only. The practical prescription is equal training for functions where aptitude exists, despite expected ridicule at unconventional spectacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal family and controlled breeding for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians will dwell in common houses, share meals, and there will be community of wives and children with state-regulated mating and selective breeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage prescribes hymeneal festivals, pairing by lots engineered by rulers so that 'the brave and the fair' unite, offspring of the good reared and others destroyed or removed; parentage is concealed and nursing organized to prevent recognition. The rulers may employ contrived chance to maintain social unity and population quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of state-sponsored falsehoods ('noble lie')
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers must sometimes use a 'strong dose of falsehood' (noble lie) as a tool to bring about desirable unions and maintain order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentator notes the need for rulers to act as 'skilful physicians of the State' who may deploy intentional untruths to secure social engineering (e.g., attributing mating outcomes to chance while orchestrating pairings). This is presented as a pragmatic, if morally fraught, instrument of governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as health of the soul; vice as disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is the health, beauty and well-being of the soul; vice is its disease, weakness and deformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses a medical metaphor: just as healthy practices produce health, just practices produce justice. A just soul/state is harmonious and well-ordered; injustice is disorderly and destructive like a disease.
